chapter: Piano craft and the New York school
title: Ellis Larkins as accompanist
summary: He praises Larkins's touch, tonal sensitivity and discipline behind singers, and the school with Don Abney.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: I suppose what you're talking of with Ellis Larkins, that's why a lot of singers liked him as an accompanist, isn't it?

Oh yeah. He's very sensitive. He's very sensitive, very beautiful. He has a magic touch on the piano. But he's not dynamic, he's not rhythmic per se -- but he's rhythmic, you know. There are rhythmic structures there, but the beauty is much...

Well, it's funny, because they recently reissued a record he made in 1943 playing one session with Coleman Hawkins and the next is with Lester Young. Now, in those days he was swinging quite hard. But later on, today on the records he makes, he hardly swings.

Well, the thing is about it, he's a tonal expert. His tonality is what... And then his discipline behind the melody line. Say, if the voice is not carrying the melody, he will beautify the voice by playing an interval that's consonant with the voice.
I guess the average person hears but does not appreciate.

No. See, when I came up, there was him and Don Abney -- he's another one... That's another school of piano playing that I was exposed to. And I borrowed whatever I could from Ellis, you know... In that way I became a little popular with some singers.
I see. Actually, we've taken you roughly to about 1933 or so, isn't it.
Ellis came into being ...(?)... My turn arrived in the Forties.
